ctx-name.prompt: A friend says: “Comte invented ‘sociology’ in anger because Quetelet had grabbed the name ‘social physics’.” What does Comte’s 1839 footnote allow you to say about this claim?
options: It confirms the claim; the footnote openly reproaches Quetelet.
It neither confirms nor refutes the claim; the footnote states that the new word is needed and equivalent to the old name, and never mentions Quetelet.
It refutes the claim, because the footnote presents ‘sociology’ as an old Latin term.
The footnote is only about the word ‘altruism’.
ctx-name.explain: The document we have (the footnote) says the term is ‘new’, ‘necessary’ and equivalent to ‘social physics’; it does not reproach a rival. So the claim cannot be confirmed from the document, but it is not ‘refuted’ either, because the story circulates in other accounts. The third option says the opposite of the footnote (the term is presented as new); the fourth confuses another word, ‘altruism’, which Comte coined later.

ctx-centuries.prompt: According to Simmel, what is the shared basic motive of the eighteenth century’s call to ‘be freed from bonds’ and the nineteenth century’s demand to ‘specialise and be unique’?
options: The wish for the state to withdraw from every field.
The individual’s resistance to being levelled and used up in a social-technical mechanism.
The wish to put religion back at the centre of society.
The wish to reverse industry and return to village life.
ctx-centuries.explain: Simmel sums up the two centuries as the individual’s resistance to being ‘levelled’ and consumed. The first option reads the eighteenth century’s call for freedom as too political; the third and fourth options are not in Simmel’s summary, which on the contrary takes the division of labour and the metropolis as an unavoidable ground.

people-cast.prompt: True or false: Durkheim and Simmel were born in the same year, and both were older than Tönnies.
people-cast.explain: The first half is true: both were born in 1858. But Tönnies was born in 1855, three years before them, so he is the older. Reversing the birth-year order is a classic exam trap: the word ‘founder’ can push you towards ‘oldest’, yet in this group the oldest is Tönnies (Comte and Spencer belong to an earlier generation).

people-press.prompt: In Weber’s 1910 proposal, ‘measuring with scissors and compass’ most resembles which of today’s research operations?
options: Running a questionnaire survey of readers.
Counting how newspaper content is distributed across sections and tracking it over time; that is, the quantitative step of content analysis.
Conducting in-depth interviews with journalists.
Having newspaper circulation figures verified in court.
people-press.explain: Weber proposes first to measure quantitatively how the content of newspapers (advertising, arts pages, leading article, news) has shifted across generations, and then to move to qualitative analysis; this resembles what we now call content analysis. Surveys and interviews may appear in other parts of the plan (journalists’ origins, reading habits), but they are not what the ‘scissors and compass’ phrase refers to; the court belongs to the end of the project, not its method.

claim-core.prompt: A researcher asks: “Are there shared values or commitments that bind social-media users to one another?” Which strand of the classical inheritance is this question closest to?
options: The integration question (what holds society together)
The question of the individual’s autonomy in front of structure
The question of anonymity in the city crowd
None of them; it is simply a new question
claim-core.explain: ‘Shared values and commitments’ is a direct extension of Durkheim’s integration question. The autonomy question would ask ‘how freely does the user choose?’; the anonymity question would ask ‘what happens in a crowd of strangers?’. The fourth option is tempting but wrong: the question is an old one in a new medium.

claim-legacy.prompt: Match each name with its counterpart in later lessons.
pairs: Social integration and the ritual reading of media events
Metropolis and stranger concepts reaching the Chicago tradition
One root of the concept of mass society
claim-legacy.explain: The pairs most often mixed up are Durkheim and Tönnies: both speak of ‘bonds’, but the one associated with the concept of mass society is Tönnies, and the one associated with integration and the ritual reading is Durkheim. Park’s study with Simmel is the documented link that carried Simmel’s urban concepts (stranger, metropolis) to Chicago.

con-social-fact.prompt: Which of the following comes closest to a social fact in Durkheim’s sense?
options: Selin falling asleep last night while watching a series
The suicide rate recorded in a given country in a given year
A newspaper’s morning editor’s mood that day
A single sentence in a novel
con-social-fact.explain: Durkheim treats rates such as marriage, birth and suicide as social facts because they are patterns that show the shared condition of a society rather than a sum of single cases. Falling asleep or an editor’s mood are individual events; a single sentence, although language is a social fact, is not by itself a social pattern.

con-solidarity.prompt: In a city, those who write, print, distribute and sell advertising for a newspaper, and those who read it, do not know one another at all, yet all depend on one another. How is this picture best labelled in Durkheim’s 1893 framework?
options: Mechanical solidarity, because the relations are impersonal.
Organic solidarity, because the bond comes from the interdependence of specialised parts.
Anomie, because nobody knows anybody.
Collective effervescence, because everyone reads the same paper.
con-solidarity.explain: The criterion of organic solidarity is not ‘acquaintance’ but ‘functional interdependence’; who knows whom does not matter. Mechanical solidarity rests on likeness (everyone does the same work, holds the same belief), not on whether relations are personal. Anomie is the loss of the authority of rules; anonymity by itself is not anomie. ‘Collective effervescence’ belongs to Durkheim’s later, ritual-centred period.

con-anomie.prompt: Imagine a community whose bonds are sound, but whose old rules have lost their authority and whose members’ desires are subject to no shared limit. Which concept in Durkheim’s main text describes this best?
options: Egoistic suicide, because bonds are weak.
Anomie, because what is weak is not integration but regulation.
Altruistic suicide, because the individual is immersed in the group.
Mechanical solidarity, because the rules rest on the past.
con-anomie.explain: In the scenario bonds are sound, so integration is in place; what is missing are shared rules limiting desires. That is the definition of anomie. Egoistic suicide arises from weak integration and altruistic suicide from excessive immersion; mechanical solidarity is a kind of bond based on likeness and has nothing to do with suicide.

con-verstehen.prompt: A researcher wants to ‘understand’, in Weber’s sense, why a group of young people spend five hours a day on social media. Which of the following comes closest to that aim?
options: Simply counting the young people’s screen time and tabulating it.
Interpreting the meaning the young people attach to this action and trying to explain it causally within means-ends relations.
Putting oneself in the young people’s place, saying ‘I would feel this way’, and stopping there.
Measuring the young people’s reaction times in a laboratory.
con-verstehen.explain: In Weber, understanding combines interpreting subjective meaning with causal explanation. A number alone gives the behaviour but not the meaning of the action; ‘I put myself in their place’ alone is empathy or intuition and does not meet Weber’s criterion of objective validity. A laboratory measurement looks at behaviour, not at the meaning of the action.

con-ideal-type.prompt: A student writes: “Weber’s ideal type is the best and truest example of a concept.” According to Weber’s definition, why is this reading wrong?
options: Because an ideal type is actually an average example.
Because an ideal type is a deliberately one-sided analytical construct; it is not found in reality as such, and its value is tested by adequacy, not by being a copy of reality.
Because an ideal type is used only in economics.
Because Weber said that the ideal type was wrong and should be abandoned.
con-ideal-type.explain: ‘Ideal’ here means ‘constructed in thought’, not ‘best’: the type is one-sidedly accentuated, is not found in reality as such, and is judged by adequacy. An average is the opposite, since an ideal type exaggerates on purpose. The third and fourth options look at Weber’s methodological discussion upside down.

con-authority.prompt: Imagine a community leader whose word is heeded, although he has no legal authority, because his followers believe he is an extraordinary person. Which of Weber’s three types is it closest to?
options: Legal-rational domination
Traditional domination
Charismatic domination
Anomic domination
con-authority.explain: The ground is devotion to the leader’s qualities that are held to be extraordinary, so it is charismatic. Had it been legal-rational, the ground would be impersonal rules and offices; had it been traditional, custom and habit. ‘Anomic domination’ is an invented option built on Durkheim’s concept of anomie; it is not in Weber’s triad.

con-rationalization.prompt: Which summary fits Weber’s rationalization thesis best?
options: Rationalization is pure progress; it only increases freedom.
Rationalization has two faces: it brings predictability and freedom, but can also lock a person in a bureaucratic cage.
Rationalization brings a revival of religions.
Rationalization affects only the economy, not culture.
con-rationalization.explain: According to the SEP author Weber is ambivalent even about the ethical consequences of rationalization: calculability increases freedom, but the same force can turn people into ‘cogs’ and beings inside a ‘cage’. The first option erases this ambivalence; the third says the opposite of disenchantment; the fourth contradicts the fact that Weber looks for rationalization in all areas of life.

con-simmel-stranger.prompt: What does Simmel’s concept of the ‘stranger’ describe?
options: A tourist who visits a country briefly and leaves.
A person who has joined a group but, not belonging to it from the start, is both near and far.
An outsider who is the group’s enemy and wants to destroy it.
A citizen of another nationality.
con-simmel-stranger.explain: Simmel explicitly sets the wanderer aside: the stranger is ‘the one who comes today and stays tomorrow’, that is, an element of the group who is at the same time positioned ‘from outside’. The tourist does not fit this definition; the enemy would be an ‘inner enemy’ type element, not one outside. Nationality is a legal concept, not Simmel’s sociological form of relation.

con-metropolis.prompt: According to Simmel, why does the metropolitan dweller develop a ‘blasé’ (dulled) attitude?
options: Because the city dweller is less intelligent.
Because stimuli change so rapidly and contradictorily that the nerves stop reacting; and because the money economy blurs the differences between things.
Because morals have collapsed in the city.
Because the city dweller has never known rural life.
con-metropolis.explain: Simmel names two sources: the rapid and contradictory flow of stimuli (a physiological source) and the money economy that reduces differences to one measure. The stupidity explanation is wrong because Simmel says the opposite; moral collapse and ignorance of the countryside are not explanatory elements in Simmel’s essay.

con-tonnies.prompt: Which of the following relations comes closest to Tönnies’s ideal type of Gesellschaft (society)?
options: The emotional bonds within a family.
A business relationship in which two parties are bound by contract for a specific purpose.
The closeness of neighbours who grew up in the same district.
The shared bond of belief in a religious community.
con-tonnies.explain: Gesellschaft is the product of elective will (Kürwille): means chosen for an end, the contract. Family, neighbourhood and spiritual community are Tönnies’s examples of Gemeinschaft. But a caution: these are ideal types, that is, not ‘pure’; a family can contain functional elements too. That is why the question says ‘closest to’.

assump-organism.prompt: Which of the following sentences is closest to Simmel’s definition of society?
options: Society is an organism that determines the life of its parts.
Society is a reality of its own kind (sui generis), irreducible to individuals.
Society is the sum of the reciprocal interactions and interdependences between individuals.
Society begins where the division of labour disappears.
assump-organism.explain: Simmel defines society not as a substance or organism but as a sum of interactions (Wechselwirkung). ‘Organism’ belongs to Spencer and ‘sui generis reality’ to Durkheim; the fourth option is the view of none of these three names.

assump-conflict.prompt: Which of the following questions is closer to the Marx line (ideology and interest)?
options: What shared value does this broadcast reaffirm, and how does it unite the community?
Which class’s idea does this broadcast make dominant, and who holds the means of mental production?
Which meanings does this broadcast lead individuals to interpret?
Through which kind of ‘will’ do the viewers of this broadcast come together?
assump-conflict.explain: ‘The ruling ideas are the ideas of the ruling class’ and ‘the means of mental production’ are Marx and Engels’s ideology line. The first option is Durkheim’s integration question, the third Weber’s question of meaning, the fourth Tönnies’s question of will.

how-suicide.prompt: Put the logical order of Durkheim’s Suicide inquiry in sequence.
items: Move from single cases to the social rate
Test the extra-social explanations one by one and eliminate them
Compare social milieus and derive the types
how-suicide.explain: First the definition, then the move to the rate, then the elimination of extra-social explanations, and finally the comparison of social milieus and the derivation of the types. Putting the types first is the typical mistake: Durkheim derives the types from the result, after elimination and comparison.

how-coronation-lab.prompt: What is Lukes’s objection in his 1975 article to ‘neo-Durkheimian’ analyses of the Shils–Young kind?
options: They exaggerate the effect of television.
They use too simple a notion of social integration and do not see the cognitive and power dimensions of ceremonies.
He claims that they collected their data wrongly.
He says that they mistranslated Durkheim.
how-coronation-lab.explain: The abstract of Lukes’s article says these analyses use too simple a notion of integration and close off the cognitive dimension, the dimension of power; it suggests reading ceremonies as elements in the ‘mobilization of bias’ rather than in value integration. The other options are not the article’s main criticism.

evid-religion.prompt: With what, rather than with ‘being a minority’, does Durkheim explain the lower suicide rate of Catholics?
options: The Catholic church’s allowing the individual less religious individualism and integrating the group more tightly.
Catholics being richer.
Catholics keeping fewer statistics.
Catholics being less urban.
evid-religion.explain: Durkheim’s explanation is integration: less religious individualism, tighter commitment. The other options do not replace it in the text; wealth and urbanity are other variables, and how statistics are kept is not Durkheim’s reasoning.

evid-media.prompt: Why does Durkheim say, in his newspaper–imitation test, that one should look at the number of readers rather than the number of newspapers?
options: Because newspapers were no longer being read.
Because a newspaper’s power to spread depends on its readership; many little-read papers can be less influential than a single large one.
Because reader numbers were easy to measure.
Because newspapers reported only suicides.
evid-media.explain: Durkheim says that in a decentralised country there may be many newspapers but each is little read, so its power to spread stays low; a single large paper, by contrast, reaches a broad public. The third option says the opposite: Durkheim himself admits that reader numbers are hard to measure.

crit-media.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the documented direct links between the classical theorists and the media?
options: Durkheim’s 1897 proposal of a test on newspaper readers and imitation
Weber’s 1910 proposal of a sociology-of-the-press survey
Tönnies’s 1922 writing of a critique of public opinion
Simmel’s 1903 measurement of the blasé attitude of television viewers
crit-media.explain: There was no television in 1903; Simmel’s blasé attitude rests on metropolitan impressions and is an essay, not a measurement study. The other three options are direct touches on the media documented in the sources.

crit-tonnies.prompt: Imagine a student writes: “A rural village is pure Gemeinschaft, a metropolis pure Gesellschaft.” Why is this problematic on Tönnies’s approach?
options: Because Tönnies never studied villages.
Because Tönnies’s concepts are ideal types; there is no pure case, and the distinction rests on the kind of will, not on place.
Because metropolises are always Gemeinschaft.
Because the concept of Gesellschaft does not belong to the nineteenth century.
crit-tonnies.explain: Tönnies’s distinction is built on two kinds of will (Wesenwille, Kürwille); the concepts are ideal types and no concrete place is ‘pure’. Equating ‘village = Gemeinschaft’ is a reading that, as our source notes, rural sociologists fell into at first and then refined. The other options are not supported in the sources.

crit-consensus.prompt: What is the main objection of Lukes’s 1975 article to ‘neo-Durkheimian’ analyses such as Shils and Young’s?
options: That they gave no place at all to ceremonies.
That they conceive social integration too simply and do not see the power-related dimension of ceremonies.
That they had not read Durkheim.
That they never mentioned television.
crit-consensus.explain: The abstract of Lukes’s article finds the notion of integration ‘too simple’ and stresses the cognitive, power dimension of ceremonies. The first and third options are unfounded (these studies do treat ceremonies and openly cite Durkheim); the fourth is not the article’s subject.

today-feed-lab.prompt: In this exercise you concluded ‘my feed felt grey throughout’. What is the most accurate way to describe it?
options: Proof of Simmel’s finding.
Your own observation; a reading that extends an idea Simmel wrote as an urban essay to today; but not a finding.
A conclusion Weber tried to prove in 1910.
A definitive scientific law.
today-feed-lab.explain: The exercise is self-observation: Simmel’s text is an essay and Weber’s text is a research plan; neither gives a finding about your feed. Calling it ‘proof’, ‘a conclusion Weber tried to prove’ or a ‘law’ would erase that distinction.

turkey-gokalp.prompt: According to the TDV Encyclopedia of Islam, which statement about Ziya Gökalp’s relation to Durkheim is the most accurate?
options: Gökalp adopted Durkheim blindly.
Gökalp was influenced by Durkheim and followed his method; but it would not be right to say he adopted him blindly.
Gökalp was opposed to Durkheim.
Gökalp followed only Weber.
turkey-gokalp.explain: The entry says both that Durkheim’s influence on Gökalp’s sociology was substantial and that this influence was not blind adoption. The first option ignores the second half, the third the first half; the fourth is not in the sources.

exam-patterns.prompt: An exam asks: “Which thinker argued that social facts should be treated as ‘things’, and in which year did he first publish this as a methodological rule?” The correct answer?
options: Comte, 1839
Durkheim, 1895
Weber, 1904
Simmel, 1908
exam-patterns.explain: Treating social facts as things is the fundamental rule of Durkheim’s Rules of Sociological Method (1895). Comte is the coiner of the term sociology (1839), Weber is associated with the ideal type and Verstehen, and Simmel with forms of sociation and the stranger.

summary.prompt: True or false: Weber’s ideal type is the best and truest example of a phenomenon.
summary.explain: False. An ideal type is a deliberately one-sided analytical construct; it is not found in reality as such, and its value is tested by adequacy. ‘Ideal’ means ‘constructed in thought’, not ‘best’.

quiz.prompt: Which thinker coined the word “sociology”, and in which work and year does it appear?
options: Durkheim, The Rules of Sociological Method, 1895
Spencer, Principles of Sociology, 1876
Comte, Cours de philosophie positive, fourth volume, 1839
Weber, Economy and Society, 1921
quiz.explain: The word is presented as a new term in a footnote in the 1839 fourth volume of Comte’s Cours. Durkheim and Weber belong to the generation after Comte and did not coin the word; Spencer is not its creator either, but the creator of the phrase ‘survival of the fittest’.

quiz.prompt: True or false: In Suicide Durkheim argued that suicide never spreads from individual to individual.
quiz.explain: False. Durkheim writes that he is sure suicide is contagious from individual to individual; in his view imitation is not strong enough to determine the social suicide rate. Separating the two claims is the key both in exams and in the newspaper–suicide debate.

quiz.prompt: Match each thinker with the concept he is most associated with.
pairs: The stranger and the blasé attitude
quiz.explain: The pair most often confused is Durkheim–Weber: both wrote about ‘authority/legitimacy’ and ‘social order’, but anomie and the social fact are Durkheim’s concepts, the ideal type and Verstehen Weber’s. Wesenwille–Kürwille are Tönnies’s two kinds of will; Simmel’s stranger and blasé attitude come from his metropolis writings.

quiz.prompt: Put the following events in chronological order (earliest to latest).
items: Comte: the fourth volume containing the word “sociologie” (1839)
Weber: the proposal of a press survey at the German Sociological Society (1910)
Shils and Young: the meaning of the coronation (1953)
quiz.explain: The order is 1839, 1887, 1897, 1903, 1910, 1953. It helps to remember that Tönnies came before Durkheim and Simmel (1887): he is the oldest of this generation. Weber’s press proposal is seven years after Simmel’s metropolis essay.

quiz.text: For Durkheim, weak integration gives rise to {{1}} suicide and weak regulation to {{2}} suicide; the fourth type, {{3}} suicide, does not appear in the main text and is mentioned only in a footnote.

options: altruistic
egoistic
anomic
egoistic
altruistic
anomic
altruistic
fatalistic
egoistic

quiz.explain: Egoistic suicide arises from weak integration and anomic suicide from weak regulation; fatalistic suicide arises from excessive regulation and appears in Suicide only in a footnote. Altruistic suicide is one of the three main types but is related not to weak integration but to excessive immersion.

quiz.scenario: Imagine a public broadcaster airs live all day on a national day of mourning; the streets are empty, people watch together at home. Two researchers interpret the broadcast separately.

parts.prompt: The first researcher says “The broadcast reaffirms a shared value and integrates society.” Which classical strand is this reading closest to?
options: Durkheim’s ritual and integration reading
Weber’s Verstehen
Simmel’s figure of the stranger
parts.explain: The reaffirmation of shared values and social integration is the central idea of the Durkheim line (and of Shils and Young’s 1953 reading). Weber’s Verstehen deals with the meaning of individual action, Simmel’s stranger with the figure of nearness and distance; integration is not their main question.

parts.prompt: The second researcher says “Integration is too simple a notion; we should look at whom the broadcast leaves out and which interest it brings forward.” Whom does this objection resemble most?
options: Comte’s law of three stages
Criticisms of the Birnbaum (1955) and Lukes (1975) kind
Tönnies’s Wesenwille
parts.explain: Birnbaum argued that divergence and tension are normal; Lukes argued that neo-Durkheimian readings use integration too simply. Comte’s law of three stages and Tönnies’s Wesenwille are not part of this debate.

parts.prompt: What is the most sensible first step in testing both claims?
options: Looking only at the audience figures
Looking at which of the two researchers is more famous
Recording together what events the broadcast covers and how, and what meaning the audience attaches to it
parts.explain: Weber’s 1910 plan proposed first a quantitative measurement of content and then qualitative analysis; ‘Verstehen’ requires taking into account the meaning attached by the audience as well. Audience figures alone show neither integration nor bias; fame is not evidence.

quiz.takeaway: The same broadcast is open to both an integration and an interest/power reading; both have to be tested together with content and audience data.

quiz.prompt: What does the footnote in the 1947 Henderson–Parsons translation say about Weber’s word Herrschaft?
options: That it should always be translated as ‘sovereignty’.
That it has no satisfactory English equivalent; ‘imperative control’ serves for general use and ‘authority’ where it is legitimate.
That it means only ‘power’.
That it cannot be translated and must never be rendered into English.
quiz.explain: The footnote says that the word has no satisfactory English equivalent, that they borrowed the term ‘imperative control’ for general use, and that for legitimate Herrschaft ‘authority’ is both accurate and less awkward. ‘Power’ is kept for Macht, not for Herrschaft.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of Weber’s three types of legitimate domination (authority)?
options: Traditional
Charismatic
Legal-rational
Mechanical
quiz.explain: Weber’s triad is traditional, charismatic and legal-rational. ‘Mechanical’ comes from Durkheim’s concept of mechanical solidarity; in exams two names and two triads are often confused.

quiz.scenario: Imagine Arda has just moved to a large city. In the mornings he sees hundreds of faces but speaks to no one. One night, on an anonymous forum, he writes to strangers something he has told nobody.

parts.prompt: According to Simmel’s 1903 essay, which concept best describes the city dweller’s attitude towards the crowd?
options: Mechanical solidarity
Charismatic domination
The reserved attitude (Reserviertheit)
parts.explain: Simmel writes that if the city dweller tried to respond inwardly to countless people he would split apart psychologically, so he develops a reserved attitude. Mechanical solidarity and charismatic domination are concepts of other thinkers.

parts.prompt: How can Arda’s anonymous confession be related to Simmel’s 1908 figure of the ‘stranger’?
options: Simmel measured an increase in confession on online forums.
Simmel said that confession is never made to a stranger.

Simmel writes that confessions withheld from those close to us are sometimes made to the stranger, especially the one passing through; this reading extended to the online setting is an interpretation.
parts.explain: Simmel’s text records that to the stranger (especially the one passing through) openness is shown that is withheld from those close; the online setting did not exist in Simmel’s time, so the link is an interpretation.

parts.prompt: What is the status of this link?
options: A documented finding of Simmel’s
An interpretation; not Simmel’s finding
A law of Tönnies’s
parts.explain: Simmel wrote about neither the online setting nor forums; this reading is our interpretation. A ‘law’ appears nowhere in this lesson; Tönnies’s ideal types are not laws either.

quiz.takeaway: Extending a classical concept to a present-day situation can be useful, but one should say that it is an interpretation.

quiz.prompt: Which of the following is true according to the abstract of Phillips’s (1974) article?
options: The stories had no effect on suicides.
The rise was seen evenly across the country, unrelated to where the story was published.
In Britain and the United States between 1947 and 1968, suicides rose immediately after suicide stories published in newspapers; the more space given to the story, the larger the rise.
The study recalculated Durkheim’s 1897 data.
quiz.explain: The abstract reports a rise immediately after the story, a larger rise after stories given more space, and a rise largely confined to the area where the story was published. The first and second options say the opposite; the fourth confuses Phillips’s data with Durkheim’s.

quiz.prompt: Which is the correct interpretation of Durkheim’s rule “treat social facts as things”?
options: Using people like objects.
Treating social facts as data given to observation, independently of personal opinions.
Holding that social facts are physical objects.
Ignoring the individual’s inner world.
quiz.explain: Durkheim’s text defines a ‘thing’ as whatever is given to observation and imposes itself on it, and equates treating facts as things with treating them as the starting data of science. The first and third options read a concept whose name is ‘thing’ literally; the fourth rests on the cliché that Durkheim ignored the individual.

quiz.prompt: True or false: The press survey Weber proposed in 1910 was completed and became the German Sociological Society’s first big publication.
quiz.explain: False. In 1912 Weber said that the enterprise had suffered a “very special ill fortune”; according to Lepsius he abandoned the project in 1911. The plan therefore went down in history as a research programme that was never carried out.
